title: What the trials show
goal: Read the block vs traditional trials and meta-analysis for endurance athletes, and grade the evidence honestly.

steps.title: The cycling trials
steps.text:
Most evidence comes from Rønnestad's group in Norway. In both trials, block and traditional groups did the **same total hours and the same number of interval sessions**: only the order changed.

| trial | block group | traditional group | VO2max change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 weeks, trained cyclists | 5 [HIIT](g:hiit) sessions in week 1, then 1 a week (n = 10) | 2 a week (n = 9) | +4.6% vs no change [[c:per-ev-4wk]] |
| 12 weeks, well-trained cyclists | same, every 4th week (n = 8) | 2 a week (n = 7) | +8.8% vs +3.7% [[c:per-ev-12wk]] |

Both favour blocks. But groups of 7–10 riders weren't randomised, and outcomes were lab tests, not races.

claims.text: In a 4-week trial, block-periodised HIIT raised VO2max by 4.6% while volume-matched traditional training gave no change.

evidence.quote: While BP increased VO2max , peak power output (Wmax) and power output at 2 mmol/L [la(-)] by 4.6 ± 3.7%, 2.1 ± 2.8%, and 10 ± 12%, respectively (P < 0.05), no changes occurred in TRAD.

claims.text: Over 12 weeks, block periodisation raised VO2max by 8.8% against 3.7% for traditional organisation.

evidence.quote: BP achieved a larger relative improvement in VO2max than TRAD (8.8 ± 5.9% vs 3.7 ± 2.9%, respectively, < 0.05)

steps.title: From a percent change to mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
steps.problem: A rider in the 4-week block group starts at a VO2max of 62 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ and gains the group's average 4.6%. What is his new VO2max?
steps: A percent change multiplies the starting value: change = 62 × 4.6 ÷ 100.
The ± 3.7% spread around that average means some riders gained almost nothing and others about 8%.

steps.title: Skiers: one yes, one no
steps.text:
Elite cross-country skiers did 5 weeks of block or traditional HIIT, again matched for total load (n = 10 vs 9). The block group raised [peak power output](g:peak-power-output) by 4% while the traditional group lost 3%, and VO2max rose 2% with blocks only [[c:per-ev-skiers]].

A [crossover study](g:crossover-study) of 20 junior skiers, men and women, compared 9 HIIT sessions packed into one week of a 3-week period with 3 a week. It found **no difference** in VO2max, 600 m time trial, economy or muscle markers [[c:per-ev-mcgawley]].

So the block advantage doesn't show up in every group, design or length of block.

claims.text: In elite skiers, 5 weeks of block-periodised HIIT raised peak power by 4% (vs −3% traditional) and VO2max by 2%.

evidence.quote: BP achieved a larger relative increase in peak power output and power output at a blood lactate concentration of 4 mmol/L than TRAD (4 ± 4 vs -3 ± 6% and 11 ± 10 vs 2 ± 4%, respectively, both P < 0.01).

claims.text: In junior skiers, block-distributed HIIT gave no extra benefit over evenly distributed HIIT.

evidence.quote: However, the findings do not support block-distributed HIT as a superior method to a more even distribution of HIT in terms of enhancing physiological or performance adaptions.

steps.title: The meta-analysis
steps.text:
Mølmen and colleagues (2019) screened 2905 records, kept 20 studies, and could pool only 6 [[c:per-ev-meta]]:

- VO2max: standardised mean difference 0.40, [95% CI](g:confidence-interval) 0.02 to 0.79, favouring blocks;
- peak power: 0.28, CI 0.01 to 0.54.

Both are **small** effects (like a [Cohen's d](g:cohens-d) of 0.3–0.4), and both intervals nearly touch zero. The 10 controlled trials it rated scored 3.7 out of 10 on average on the PEDro scale, a 10-point checklist of how well a trial was run [[c:per-ev-quality]]. The pooled studies lasted 4.9 weeks on average (1–12 weeks).

A limit to keep in mind: Rønnestad, the review's last (senior) author, was first author of 4 of the 6 pooled trials [[c:per-ev-authors]]. That's common in a small field, and the authors declared no conflicts of interest, but an independent review would add confidence.

claims.text: Pooled, block periodisation had small favourable effects on VO2max (SMD 0.40) and peak power (SMD 0.28) compared with traditional organisation.

evidence.quote: The meta-analyses revealed small favorable effects for BP compared to TRAD regarding changes in VO2max (standardized mean difference, 0.40; 95% CI=0.02, 0.79) and Wmax (standardized mean difference, 0.28; 95% CI=0.01, 0.54).

claims.text: The block periodisation studies were small and of generally low methodological quality.

evidence.quote: these results must be considered with some caution due to small studies with generally low methodological quality (mean PEDro score =3.7/10).

claims.text: Rønnestad is the last author of the meta-analysis and first author of 4 of its 6 pooled trials; the authors declared no conflicts of interest.

evidence.quote: Six of the 20 studies were eligible for meta-analysis (ie, parallel-design studies comparing BP with TRAD).
Rønnestad BR, Hansen J, Thyli V, Bakken TA, Sandbakk O. 5-week block periodization increases aerobic power in elite cross-country skiers.
The authors report no conflicts of interest in this work.

steps.title: Grading it honestly

claims.text: The evidence that block periodisation beats traditional organisation is small, short and low in quality.

evidence.quote: Nonetheless, the number of eligible studies are quite small (n=10) and they achieved only low-to-moderate PEDro scores.
However, the long-term effects of this organization may not directly be answered by the relatively short-term studies conducted so far in the literature.
More or less all studies are at a higher risk of bias, mostly because of lack of blinding of testers and specifying randomization

points: Block and traditional groups in the trials did the same total load: only the order of the intervals changed.
Cycling trials (n = 7–10 per group) and one skier trial favoured blocks; a crossover in junior skiers found no difference.
The meta-analysis: small effects (SMD 0.40 VO2max, 0.28 peak power), CIs near zero, quality 3.7/10, studies of about 5 weeks.
Grade: weak. Blocks are a reasonable option, not a proven upgrade; season-long effects are unknown.
Reverse periodisation: no advantage shown, also weak evidence.

variants.stem: In the block vs traditional cycling trials, why did the groups do the same total hours and number of interval sessions?

options.text: So any difference could be put down to the order of sessions
options.why: Right: matching the load isolates the effect of how it is organised.

options.text: So both groups would gain exactly the same
options.why: Matching the inputs doesn't force equal outcomes; it lets you compare them fairly.

options.text: Because random allocation was impossible otherwise
options.why: Matching load and random allocation are separate design choices; these trials weren't randomised.

options.text: To make the study blind to the riders
options.why: Riders could see how many intervals they did; load matching doesn't blind them.

variants.stem: A cyclist with a VO2max of 58 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ gains the 4-week block group's average of 4.6%. What is his new VO2max?

options.text: 60.7 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
62.6 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: That adds 4.6 as if it were mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, not a percentage.

options.text: 84.7 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: That multiplies by 1.46: a 46% gain, not 4.6%.

options.text: 55.3 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: That subtracts the change instead of adding it.

variants.stem: Two riders both start at 60 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Over 12 weeks one gains 8.8% (block), the other 3.7% (traditional). How far apart are they after?

options.text: About 3.1 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
About 5.1 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: That takes the difference in percent (5.1) as if it were mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹.

options.text: About 5.3 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: That's the block rider's whole gain, forgetting the traditional rider also improved.

options.text: About 0.3 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: That treats 8.8% and 3.7% as 0.88% and 0.37%: a decimal slip (0.53 − 0.22).

variants.stem: A skier's peak power on the ramp test is 380 W. After 5 weeks she gains the block group's average 4%. What is her new peak power?

options.text: About 395 W

options.why: That adds 4 W, treating the percent as watts.

options.text: About 532 W
options.why: That multiplies by 1.4: a 40% gain.

options.text: About 369 W
options.why: That applies the traditional group's −3% instead.

variants.solution: Change = 380 × 4 ÷ 100 = 15.2 W. New peak power ≈ 395 W.

variants.stem: What did the crossover study in 20 junior cross-country skiers find for block vs evenly spread HIIT?

options.text: No difference in fitness or performance
options.why: Right: no differences in VO2max, time trial, economy or muscle markers.

options.text: A clear advantage for blocks
options.why: That was the elite skier and cyclist trials, not this one.

options.text: A clear advantage for even spreading
options.why: Neither way was better; the 600 m time trial improved after both.

options.text: More illness and fatigue in the block period
options.why: Recovery and stress scores didn't differ between the periods.

variants.stem: One 5-week trial in elite skiers favours blocks; a 3-week crossover in junior skiers finds no difference. What is the most reasonable conclusion?

options.text: Any block advantage isn't robust across groups and designs
options.why: Right: mixed results from small studies mean the effect, if real, is small or depends on context.

options.text: The crossover is wrong because it disagrees with the trial
options.why: A crossover with 20 athletes is no weaker by design; disagreement means uncertainty.

options.text: Blocks work in elite athletes only, which is now proven
options.why: Two small studies can't prove an interaction with training level.

options.text: The trial is wrong because elite athletes can't improve
options.why: Elite athletes can improve; the study's design, not their level, is what limits it.

variants.stem: The pooled effect of blocks on VO2max was 0.40, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.79. What does the interval tell you?

options.text: The true effect may be near zero or moderate
options.why: Right: the interval runs from barely above zero to about 0.8.

options.text: Blocks raise VO2max by 0.40 to 0.79%
options.why: These are standardised effect sizes, not percent changes.

options.text: The effect is large and certain
options.why: 0.40 is small, and a lower end of 0.02 is close to no effect.

options.text: There's a 95% chance blocks are worse
options.why: The whole interval is above zero, favouring blocks, if only just.

variants.stem: What most limits the meta-analysis claiming blocks beat traditional training?

options.text: Few small, short, low-quality trials, many by the authors' own group
options.why: Right: 6 pooled studies, PEDro 3.7/10, about 5 weeks long, several led by its senior author.

options.text: It pooled too many studies to be precise
options.why: It pooled only 6; more studies would make it more precise, not less.

options.text: Its interval excludes zero, so it can't be trusted
options.why: An interval that excludes zero is a point in its favour, though only just here.

options.text: It measured race results, which are too noisy
options.why: It pooled lab measures (VO2max, peak power), not races.

variants.stem: Using the course's rubric, what grade fits "block periodisation beats traditional organisation for endurance athletes"?

options.text: Weak
options.why: Right: few small, mostly non-randomised, short trials in mostly trained men.

options.text: Strong
options.why: A meta-analysis alone isn't enough: strong needs consistent reviews of good trials.

options.text: Moderate
options.why: Moderate needs several agreeing RCTs; these are small, mostly not randomised, and one disagrees.

options.text: Disputed
options.why: There is one null study, but most point the same way; the problem is quality, not a clash of good studies.

variants.stem: Why can 4-week trials not tell you whether block periodisation is better across a whole season?

options.text: Gains over a few weeks may not add up or last over months
options.why: Right: short-term effects say nothing about how they accumulate over a season.

options.text: Four weeks is too short for any training adaptation
options.why: VO2max can change within weeks; the trials did show changes.

options.text: Season-long trials always find the opposite
options.why: There are no season-long trials to compare with.

options.text: Lab tests cannot measure VO2max properly
options.why: Lab tests measure VO2max well; the issue is the time frame.

variants.stem: A runner training 7 hours a week asks whether to switch to a block plan of 5 interval sessions in one week, then 1 a week for three weeks. What's the fairest answer?

options.text: It's a reasonable option to try, not a proven upgrade
options.why: Right: evidence is weak, small and short; trying it and watching the response is fair.

options.text: Yes: blocks are proven to beat traditional plans
options.why: The evidence is weak, with one null trial; "proven" overstates it.

options.text: No: blocks are proven to cause overtraining
options.why: No trial showed harm; junior skiers coped with 9 sessions in a week.

options.text: Only if he also doubles his weekly hours
options.why: In the trials, total load stayed the same; only the order changed.
